metadata.title: SDE Master Learning & Interview Preparation Platform
metadata.description: A dependency-driven, beginner-to-advanced Software Development Engineer (SDE) learning platform with Google/Gmail & Email authentication and database persistence.

readinessRubric.label: Unfamiliar
readinessRubric.description: Have not studied the concept yet.

readinessRubric.label: Recognize It
readinessRubric.description: Know the definition and where it fits, but need notes to explain details.

readinessRubric.label: Explain with Notes
readinessRubric.description: Understand mechanics and basic use cases; can walk through with reference material.

readinessRubric.label: Explain & Apply Unaided
readinessRubric.description: Can explain core idea in 1-2 minutes without notes, implement it, and handle edge cases (Target for all Must-Learn P0 topics).

readinessRubric.label: Defend Trade-offs
readinessRubric.description: Can compare alternatives, analyze time/memory/operational trade-offs, and defend design under interview pressure.

readinessChecklist: I can explain the core idea without notes in 1-2 minutes.
I can name a realistic use case and when not to use it.
I can compare alternatives and explain time, memory, cost, or operational trade-offs.
I can describe edge cases, failure modes, and mitigations.
I can implement it, solve a related problem, or diagram it where applicable.
I can handle follow-up questions and communicate uncertainty clearly.

phases.title: Phase 1: Programming Foundations
phases.subtitle: Syntax, memory model, OOP basics, recursion, and asymptotic complexity
phases.summary: Establishes fluency in a core programming language (Python, Java, C++, or Go), execution memory model (Stack vs. Heap), recursion, exception handling, and Big-O complexity analysis before tackling data structures.
phases.whyThisOrder: Every data structure, algorithm, and system component is expressed in code. Mastering control flow, memory layout, recursion, and Big-O notation first prevents rote memorization in Phase 2.

topics.title: Programming Fundamentals & Language Mechanics
topics.summary: Covers variables, primitive and reference types, control flow, type systems, and programming paradigms (imperative, procedural, declarative, event-driven).
topics.whyImportant: Writing bug-free interview code requires deep familiarity with how your primary language handles types, mutability, pass-by-value vs. reference, and scoping.

subtopics.name: Variables, primitive types, and control flow (conditionals, loops, short-circuiting)
Static vs. Dynamic typing & Strong vs. Weak typing
Nominal vs. Structural typing
Programming paradigms: Imperative, Procedural, Declarative, and Event-driven
Regular expressions: pattern matching, capture groups, and pitfalls

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook — Programming Languages for Interviews
Coding Interview University — Choose a Language

exercises: Implement custom string/number parsers, FizzBuzz variants, and matrix traversal utilities without library helpers.
Write a CLI log parser using regular expressions to extract timestamps, severity levels, and error codes.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between static/dynamic typing and strong/weak typing? Give examples.
How does your primary interview language pass primitives vs. objects/arrays to functions?
topics.interviewRelevance: Tested implicitly in every coding round; interviewers evaluate idiomatic usage of standard library types and mutability rules.
topics.completionCriteria: Can write clean loops, conditionals, type conversions, and string manipulations in your primary language without syntax lookups.

topics.title: Functions, Call Stack & Functional Concepts
topics.originalSection: 9. Problem-solving and Coding / 10. Programming Languages and Concepts
topics.summary: Covers function execution frames, base cases and recursive decomposition, tail recursion, closures, and higher-order functions.
topics.whyImportant: Recursion is the direct foundation for trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer, backtracking, and dynamic programming.

subtopics.name: Call stack frames, base cases, and recursive leap of faith
Tail recursion and stack overflow prevention
Lambda expressions, closures, pure functions, and higher-order functions
Referential transparency and immutability
Mutual recursion, anonymous recursion, and Lambda calculus basics

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook — Coding Round Prep

exercises: Trace the call stack tree by hand for Fibonacci(5), Factorial(5), and Tower of Hanoi(3).
Convert 3 recursive functions (sum of digits, array reversal, power function) into iterative and tail-recursive forms.
interviewQuestions: What happens in memory when a recursive function lacks a reachable base case?
What is tail-call optimization and why do some languages (like Python/Java) not support it natively?
topics.interviewRelevance: Essential prerequisite for tree traversals, DFS, divide and conquer, and memoization.
topics.completionCriteria: Can trace recursive call trees, identify stack depth, and convert simple recursion to iteration using an explicit stack.

topics.title: Memory Layout & Garbage Collection
topics.summary: Explains how programs organize memory across code, data, stack, and heap segments, and how automatic garbage collectors reclaim memory.
topics.whyImportant: Understanding stack vs. heap allocation explains pointer semantics, object overhead, memory leaks, and latency spikes in production services.

subtopics.name: Stack vs. Heap memory allocation and lifetimes
Data segment vs. Code segment
Manual vs. Automatic memory management
Tracing (Mark and Sweep) vs. Reference counting garbage collection
Generational Garbage Collection (Young/Old generations, stop-the-world pauses)

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP) — Memory API

exercises: Create a diagram showing where local variables, object fields, static constants, and closures live in memory.
Demonstrate a reference cycle in Python/JS and show how a cycle detector or weak reference resolves it.
interviewQuestions: Compare Stack vs. Heap allocation in terms of speed, fragmentation, thread safety, and lifetime.
Why can pure reference counting fail to reclaim memory, and how does generational GC optimize collection?
topics.interviewRelevance: Frequently asked in language deep-dives and backend performance troubleshooting interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can explain stack vs. heap trade-offs and compare reference counting with generational mark-and-sweep GC.

topics.title: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Foundations
topics.originalSection: 10. Programming Languages and Concepts / 6. Low-Level Design
topics.summary: Covers classes, objects, interfaces, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, and composition vs. inheritance.
topics.whyImportant: OOP provides the vocabulary for structuring modular code and is the direct prerequisite for Low-Level Design (Phase 5).

subtopics.name: Classes, objects, constructors, interfaces, and abstract classes
Encapsulation and access modifiers (state hiding & invariants)
Abstraction and interface contracts
Inheritance and Polymorphism (compile-time overloading vs. runtime overriding)
Composition vs. Inheritance: why to favor composition over deep class hierarchies

exercises: Model a bank account hierarchy (Checking, Savings, Investment) and refactor an inheritance-heavy design to use composition.
Implement polymorphic payment processors using interfaces/abstract base classes.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface, and when do you choose each?
Why is 'favor composition over inheritance' considered a core rule in modern software design?
topics.interviewRelevance: Direct foundation for all Low-Level Design (LLD) and Object-Oriented Design rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can design clean class hierarchies, use interfaces for polymorphism, and refactor brittle inheritance into composition.

topics.title: Error Handling, Exceptions & Debugging Basics
topics.originalSection: 9. Problem-solving and Coding / 10. Programming Languages and Concepts
topics.summary: Covers exception hierarchies, error propagation, resource cleanup (try/finally/context managers), exceptions vs. error codes, and systematic debugging.
topics.whyImportant: Production-grade code and LLD solutions require predictable error handling, invariant validation, and fast root-cause debugging.

subtopics.name: Exception handling mechanisms (try/catch/finally, context managers)
Error propagation, custom domain exceptions, and error recovery
Exceptions vs. Error codes / Result types & exception safety
Debugging techniques: interactive debuggers, breakpoints, print/log debugging, rubber ducking

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook — Coding Best Practices

exercises: Write a file/socket reader with guaranteed resource cleanup under partial failure conditions.
Debug 5 buggy array/recursion programs using an interactive step debugger.
interviewQuestions: When should a function throw an exception versus returning an error value or status object?
How do you prevent resource leaks when an exception occurs mid-operation?
topics.interviewRelevance: Interviewers look for defensive input checks and clean failure handling in coding and LLD interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Consistently validates inputs, handles edge cases cleanly, and uses step debugging effectively.

topics.title: Problem-Solving Strategy & Time/Space Complexity
topics.summary: Covers asymptotic analysis (Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta), worst/average/amortized complexity, auxiliary space vs. input space, and structured problem-solving steps.
topics.whyImportant: Every coding interview ends with a complexity analysis; Big-O determines whether an algorithm scales or times out.

subtopics.name: Big O (upper bound), Big Omega (lower bound), and Big Theta (tight bound) notations
Time complexity of loops, nested loops, and recursive recurrence relations
Space complexity analysis: auxiliary heap space vs. recursion call stack space
Space-time trade-offs and amortized complexity (e.g., dynamic array resizing)
Structured problem-solving: Understand -> Plan -> Break down -> Solve simpler -> Implement -> Test

exercises: Analyze time and auxiliary space complexity for 10 code snippets including binary search, merge sort, and branching recursion.
Prove why dynamic array append is O(1) amortized despite O(N) occasional resizing.
interviewQuestions: What is the time and space complexity of a recursive function with branching factor 2 and depth N?
Explain amortized O(1) time complexity using dynamic arrays or two-stack queues.
topics.interviewRelevance: Mandatory in 100% of DSA and coding interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can state and justify exact time and space complexity (including recursion stack) for any code you write.

phases.title: Phase 2: Data Structures and Algorithms
phases.subtitle: Linear structures, hashing, sorting, trees, heaps, graphs, and algorithmic paradigms
phases.summary: Consolidated and properly sequenced from the original repository's separate 'Algorithms' (Section 2), 'Data Structures' (Section 4), and 'Problem-solving and Coding' (Section 9) sections so each data structure is learned before the algorithms that depend on it.
phases.whyThisOrder: Linear structures (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues, Hash Tables) must precede Searching/Sorting and hierarchical structures (Trees, Heaps, Tries), which in turn unlock Graphs, Greedy, Backtracking, and Dynamic Programming.

topics.title: Arrays, Strings & Two-Pointer / Sliding Window Patterns
topics.originalSection: 4. Data Structures / 2. Algorithms / 9. Problem-solving and Coding
topics.summary: Covers contiguous memory arrays, dynamic arrays, string manipulation, prefix sums, two pointers, sliding window, and Kadane's algorithm.
topics.whyImportant: Arrays and strings account for over 35% of SDE coding interview questions and form the backing storage for hash tables and heaps.

subtopics.name: Static vs. Dynamic arrays, contiguous memory indexing, and 2D matrices
Two Pointers pattern (opposite ends, same direction, partitioning)
Sliding Window pattern (fixed and variable length windows)
Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm) and Prefix Sums
String fundamentals: Palindrome check, anagram check, immutability, StringBuilder

resources.title: NeetCode Roadmap — Arrays & Hashing / Two Pointers / Sliding Window
Tech Interview Handbook — Array & String Cheatsheet

exercises: Solve Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water, and Trapping Rain Water using Two Pointers.
Solve Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters and Minimum Window Substring using Sliding Window.
Solve Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm) and Product of Array Except Self.
interviewQuestions: When can a nested O(N^2) subarray loop be reduced to O(N) with a sliding window, and when does sliding window fail (e.g., negative numbers)?
How does Kadane's algorithm handle an array containing all negative numbers?
topics.interviewRelevance: Highest-frequency category in online assessments and phone screens.
topics.completionCriteria: Can immediately recognize and code Two Pointers, Sliding Window, and Prefix Sum solutions in O(N) time.

topics.title: Linked Lists & Pointer Manipulation
topics.summary: Covers singly, doubly, and circular linked lists, dummy head nodes, in-place reversal, and Floyd's fast-and-slow pointer cycle detection.
topics.whyImportant: Tests pointer precision and underpins LRU caches, hash table chaining, deque implementations, and OS free-lists.

subtopics.name: Singly linked lists, Doubly linked lists, and Circular linked lists
Fast and slow pointers (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare cycle detection & middle finding)
In-place reversal, merging sorted lists, and dummy sentinel nodes
Skip lists (probabilistic O(log N) search)
Unrolled linked lists & Lock-free linked lists (moved from P0 to Optional/Advanced P2)

exercises: Implement Singly and Doubly Linked Lists from scratch with O(1) head/tail operations.
Solve Reverse Linked List, Merge Two Sorted Lists, Linked List Cycle II, and Reorder List.
interviewQuestions: Prove mathematically why Floyd's fast and slow pointers are guaranteed to meet inside a cycle.
Why does an LRU Cache combine a Doubly Linked List with a Hash Map?
topics.interviewRelevance: Core staple of coding interviews and required to build LRU/LFU caches in LLD.
topics.completionCriteria: Can manipulate list pointers without losing references or triggering null-pointer bugs.

topics.title: Stacks, Queues & Monotonic Structures
topics.summary: Covers LIFO stacks, FIFO queues, circular queues, double-ended queues (Deques), expression evaluation, and monotonic stacks/queues.
topics.whyImportant: Stacks power DFS, backtracking, and parsing; queues power BFS, rate buffers, and asynchronous task scheduling.

subtopics.name: Stack implementations (array-based and linked-list-based) & expression evaluation
Queue implementations, Circular queue, and BFS/scheduling applications
Double-ended queue (Deque) and sliding window maximum
Monotonic Stack (Next Greater Element, Daily Temperatures, Largest Rectangle in Histogram)
Priority stacks

exercises: Solve Valid Parentheses, Min Stack, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, and Next Greater Element.
Implement a Queue using two Stacks (amortized O(1)) and a Circular Ring Buffer.
interviewQuestions: How does a Monotonic Stack find the Next Greater Element for all N elements in O(N) time?
How do you implement a fixed-capacity Circular Queue using an array without wasting a slot?
topics.interviewRelevance: Frequently tested via Monotonic Stack and Deque sliding-window problems.
topics.completionCriteria: Can implement stack/queue ADTs and solve monotonic stack problems in O(N) time.

topics.title: Hash Tables & Probabilistic Data Structures
topics.originalSection: 4. Data Structures / 2. Algorithms / 9. Problem-solving and Coding
topics.summary: Covers hash functions, load factors, collision resolution (chaining vs. open addressing), and space-efficient probabilistic structures (Bloom Filters, Count-Min Sketch).
topics.whyImportant: Hash tables turn O(N) searches into O(1) lookups in coding problems and underpin database hash indexes and distributed caches.

subtopics.name: Hash functions, uniform distribution, load factor, and rehashing
Collision resolution: Separate Chaining vs. Open Addressing (linear/quadratic probing)
Robin Hood Hashing & Cuckoo Hashing (reclassified from P0 to P1/P2)
Bloom Filters (false positive trade-offs) & Count-Min Sketch for high-scale systems
Perfect Hashing

exercises: Implement a generic Hash Map from scratch with dynamic resizing and separate chaining.
Solve Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements, Longest Consecutive Sequence, and Subarray Sum Equals K.
interviewQuestions: What happens to Hash Map lookup complexity in the worst case, and how did Java 8+ mitigate hash collision attacks?
How does a Bloom Filter work, why can you not delete keys from a basic Bloom Filter, and where is it used in databases?
topics.interviewRelevance: Used in almost every coding interview and frequently discussed in HLD caching/storage rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can implement a hash table from scratch and use hash maps/sets to optimize O(N^2) lookups to O(N).

topics.title: Searching, Sorting & Divide-and-Conquer
topics.summary: Covers binary search on sorted arrays and monotonic answer spaces, comparison sorts (Merge, Quick, Heap, TimSort), non-comparison sorts (Counting, Radix, Bucket), and Divide & Conquer.
topics.whyImportant: Binary search and sorting are fundamental building blocks for interval merging, greedy algorithms, and database index scans.

subtopics.name: Binary Search (1D/2D arrays, Peak Element, Rotated Sorted Array, Binary Search on Answer)
Merge Sort (stable O(N log N)), Quick Sort (partitioning & pivot selection), and QuickSelect
Insertion Sort, Selection Sort, Bubble Sort, and hybrid Tim Sort
Non-comparison sorts: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, and Bucket Sort
Exponential/Ternary Search & Closest Pair of Points (Divide & Conquer)
Academic sorts & D&C: Strassen's Matrix, Karatsuba, FFT, Shell/Bitonic/Cycle/Pancake Sort

exercises: Implement Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Binary Search (lower_bound and upper_bound) without off-by-one errors.
Solve Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Peak Element, Koko Eating Bananas, and Merge Intervals.
interviewQuestions: Why is Quick Sort often faster in practice than Merge Sort for in-memory arrays, yet Merge Sort is preferred for external disk sorting?
How do you recognize when an optimization problem can be solved via 'Binary Search on Answer'?
topics.interviewRelevance: Binary search variants and interval sorting are top-tier coding interview topics.
topics.completionCriteria: Can write bug-free binary search on boundary conditions and explain stability, in-place, and time complexity of major sorts.

topics.title: Trees, Binary Search Trees & Balanced Search Trees
topics.summary: Covers binary trees, DFS (preorder, inorder, postorder) and BFS (level-order) traversals, Binary Search Trees (BST), self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black), and B/B+ Trees.
topics.whyImportant: Trees model hierarchical data (DOM, file systems, ASTs) and database indexes (B-Trees/LSM-Trees), and are heavily tested in interviews.

subtopics.name: Binary Trees: Complete, Full, and Perfect binary trees; DFS & BFS level-order traversals
Binary Search Trees (BST): validation, insertion, deletion, Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)
Self-balancing BSTs: AVL Trees (rotations) and Red-Black Trees (invariants)
B-Trees and B+ Trees (disk-page alignment and database indexing foundation)
Advanced tree variants: Splay Trees, Radix Trees, Scapegoat Trees, Tango Trees

exercises: Solve Invert Binary Tree, Maximum Depth, Diameter of Binary Tree, Binary Tree Level Order Traversal, Validate BST, and Lowest Common Ancestor.
Implement BST serialize/deserialize and iterative inorder traversal using an explicit stack.
interviewQuestions: What property makes an inorder traversal of a valid BST sorted, and how do you validate a BST in O(N) time?
Why do relational databases use B+ Trees instead of AVL or Red-Black binary trees for disk indexes?
topics.interviewRelevance: Trees are among the top 3 most tested topics in FAANG coding rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can solve recursive and iterative tree traversal problems and explain BST balancing and B+ Tree branching.

topics.title: Heaps, Priority Queues & Top-K Patterns
topics.summary: Covers binary min-heaps and max-heaps, array representation of complete binary trees, O(N) heapify, Heap Sort, and Two-Heap / Top-K patterns.
topics.whyImportant: Heaps enable O(log N) priority scheduling, Top-K streaming queries, Median maintenance, and Dijkstra's / Prim's graph algorithms.

subtopics.name: Min-Heap and Max-Heap array indexing, sift-up, sift-down, and O(N) build-heap
Heap Sort (in-place O(N log N) sorting)
Top-K elements, K-way merge, and Two-Heaps pattern (Find Median from Data Stream)

exercises: Implement a binary Min-Heap from scratch using a dynamic array.
Solve Kth Largest Element in an Array, Merge K Sorted Lists, Task Scheduler, and Find Median from Data Stream.
interviewQuestions: Why does building a heap from an unsorted array of N elements take O(N) time instead of O(N log N)?
To find the K largest elements in a stream of N items, why do you use a Min-Heap of size K instead of a Max-Heap?
topics.interviewRelevance: Essential for Top-K, streaming median, scheduling, and shortest-path graph problems.
topics.completionCriteria: Can implement a binary heap and solve Top-K, K-way merge, and Two-Heap streaming problems.

topics.title: Graphs, Traversals, Shortest Paths & Spanning Trees
topics.summary: Unifies graph representations, BFS/DFS traversals, cycle detection, topological sorting, Union-Find (DSU), shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall), and MSTs (Kruskal, Prim).
topics.whyImportant: Graphs model networks, dependencies, social graphs, and routing; they bridge core DSA and distributed system topology.

subtopics.name: Graph representations (Adjacency List, Adjacency Matrix, Edge List) & Directed/Undirected/Weighted/Bipartite graphs
Graph Traversals (BFS & DFS), Connected Components, and Cycle Detection (directed & undirected)
Topological Sorting (Kahn's BFS in-degree algorithm & DFS postorder) and Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)
Shortest Path Algorithms: Dijkstra's (non-negative weights), Bellman-Ford (negative weights), Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs)
Minimum Spanning Trees (MST): Kruskal's Algorithm and Prim's Algorithm
Planar/Eulerian graphs, Incidence matrix, and Kosaraju's Strongly Connected Components

exercises: Solve Number of Islands, Clone Graph, Course Schedule I & II (Topological Sort), Redundant Connection (Union-Find), and Network Delay Time (Dijkstra).
Implement Union-Find with path compression and union by rank.
interviewQuestions: When should you use BFS vs. Dijkstra's vs. Bellman-Ford for shortest paths?
How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph versus an undirected graph?
topics.interviewRelevance: Grid BFS/DFS, Topological Sort, Union-Find, and Dijkstra appear heavily in mid-to-senior SDE interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can fluently code BFS, DFS, Kahn's Topological Sort, Union-Find, and Dijkstra's algorithm.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms & Interval Scheduling
topics.summary: Covers greedy-choice property, optimal substructure, interval scheduling, Fractional Knapsack, Huffman coding, and exchange arguments.
topics.whyImportant: Greedy algorithms yield fast O(N log N) or O(N) solutions when local optimal choices guarantee global optimality.

subtopics.name: Greedy choice property vs. Dynamic Programming; Fractional Knapsack Problem
Activity Selection Problem, Job Sequencing with Deadlines, and Interval Scheduling
Huffman Coding (prefix-free compression trees)
Greedy Set Cover and Greedy Graph Coloring approximations

exercises: Solve Jump Game I & II, Non-overlapping Intervals, Meeting Rooms II, and Gas Station.
interviewQuestions: Why does a greedy approach work for Fractional Knapsack and Activity Selection, but fail for 0/1 Knapsack and arbitrary Coin Change?
How do you prove a greedy algorithm is optimal using an exchange argument?
topics.interviewRelevance: Interval scheduling and greedy feasibility checks are frequent coding interview questions.
topics.completionCriteria: Can distinguish greedy-solvable problems from DP problems and solve interval scheduling problems.

topics.title: Backtracking & Dynamic Programming (DP)
topics.summary: Progresses naturally from exhaustive recursive search (Backtracking with pruning) to overlapping subproblems (Top-Down Memoization and Bottom-Up Tabulation).
topics.whyImportant: Backtracking and DP represent the capstone of algorithmic problem solving in coding interviews.

subtopics.name: Backtracking: state-space tree pruning, Subsets, Permutations, Combination Sum, N-Queens
DP Foundations: Overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, Memoization (top-down) vs. Tabulation (bottom-up)
1D & Knapsack DP: Fibonacci, Climbing Stairs, Coin Change, 0/1 Knapsack, Subset Sum, Rod Cutting
String & Sequence DP: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS), Edit Distance
Interval & Matrix DP: Matrix Chain Multiplication, Grid Unique Paths

exercises: Solve Subsets, Permutations, Combination Sum, and Word Search using Backtracking.
Solve House Robber, Coin Change, Partition Equal Subset Sum, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, and Longest Increasing Subsequence.
interviewQuestions: Walk through how to transition a brute-force recursive solution to top-down memoization, bottom-up tabulation, and space-optimized DP.
What is the difference between 0/1 Knapsack and Unbounded Knapsack in the inner loop iteration order of 1D DP?
topics.interviewRelevance: Medium-to-hard DP and Backtracking questions frequently serve as the differentiator in final coding loops.
topics.completionCriteria: Can define state, transition equation, and base cases for 1D/2D DP and prune backtracking trees cleanly.

topics.title: Tries, String Matching & Bit Manipulation
topics.originalSection: 2. Algorithms / 4. Data Structures / 9. Problem-solving and Coding
topics.summary: Covers Prefix Trees (Tries), rolling string hashes, pattern matching (KMP, Rabin-Karp), bit manipulation tricks, and advanced suffix structures.
topics.whyImportant: Tries power autocomplete and IP routing; bit manipulation enables compact state representation and O(1) parity checks.

subtopics.name: Trie (Prefix Tree): insertion, prefix search, DFS/BFS in a Trie, autocomplete
Bit Manipulation: XOR properties, bitmasks, power-of-two checks, counting set bits
String Hashing, Rolling Hash (Rabin-Karp), Longest Common Prefix (LCP), Longest Palindromic Substring
Pattern Matching: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP), Z-Algorithm, Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick
Competitive String Structures: Manacher's, Suffix Array/Tree/Automaton, Burrows-Wheeler, Baker-Bird

exercises: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree) and solve Design Add and Search Words Data Structure and Word Search II.
Solve Single Number, Counting Bits, Reverse Bits, and Longest Palindromic Substring.
interviewQuestions: Compare a Trie with a Hash Set for storing 1 million dictionary words and supporting prefix autocomplete.
How does rolling hash in Rabin-Karp achieve O(N + M) expected string matching time?
topics.interviewRelevance: Tries are very common in both coding and LLD/HLD autocomplete questions; KMP/Rabin-Karp are useful for senior rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can implement a Trie from scratch and apply XOR/bitmask operations without lookup.

phases.title: Phase 3: Computer Science Fundamentals
phases.subtitle: Operating systems, concurrency, virtual memory, computer networks, SQL, and NoSQL databases
phases.summary: Unifies Operating Systems (Section 8), Concurrency & Memory (duplicated in Section 10), Networking (Sections 7 & 10), and Databases (Section 5) into the foundational systems layer required before building backend applications or distributed architectures.
phases.whyThisOrder: You cannot reason about database connection pools, thread-safe services, or distributed system bottlenecks (Phase 6) without first understanding OS processes/threads, virtual memory, TCP/HTTP networking, and relational/NoSQL storage.

topics.title: Operating Systems: Processes, Threads & Concurrency
topics.originalSection: 8. Operating Systems / 10. Programming Languages and Concepts
topics.summary: Deduplicates and unifies OS processes vs. threads, CPU scheduling, synchronization primitives (mutexes, semaphores, monitors), deadlocks, and async concurrency.
topics.whyImportant: Backend engineers write multi-threaded and asynchronous services daily; concurrency bugs (race conditions, deadlocks) are prime interview topics.

subtopics.name: Processes vs. Threads, context switching, and Parallelism vs. Concurrency
Thread safety, Race conditions, Critical sections, and Synchronization primitives (Mutexes, Semaphores, Monitors)
Deadlock conditions (Coffman conditions) and Deadlock detection, prevention, and avoidance
Asynchronous programming: Event loops, Callbacks, Promises, Futures, and Coroutines
CPU Scheduling algorithms: FIFO, Round Robin, Shortest Job First, Earliest Deadline First (EDF), Fair Share, WFQ

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP) — Virtualization & Concurrency

exercises: Implement a thread-safe Bounded Blocking Queue using a mutex and condition variables (monitors).
Write a small program that intentionally triggers a deadlock between two locks, then fix it via lock ordering.
interviewQuestions: What are the 4 necessary conditions for a deadlock, and what is the most practical way to prevent deadlocks in production code?
Explain the difference between a Mutex and a Semaphore, and between multi-threading and a single-threaded async event loop.
topics.interviewRelevance: Heavily tested in CS fundamentals rounds, concurrency coding problems, and LLD.
topics.completionCriteria: Can explain processes vs. threads, prevent race conditions and deadlocks, and implement producer-consumer synchronization.

topics.title: Virtual Memory, Paging & File Systems
topics.originalSection: 8. Operating Systems / 10. Programming Languages and Concepts
topics.summary: Covers virtual address spaces, demand paging, page tables, TLB, page replacement policies (LRU, FIFO, Clock), memory-mapped files, and local/network file systems.
topics.whyImportant: Explains how databases use `mmap` and buffer pools, why page faults hurt p99 latency, and how OS caching works.

subtopics.name: Virtual Memory, Demand Paging, Page Tables, TLB, and Page Faults
Page Replacement Algorithms: LRU, FIFO, Optimal, and Clock algorithm
Buddy memory allocation and Memory-mapped files (mmap)
File Systems: Inodes, Journaling file systems (ext3, ext4), File system encryption, and Network file systems (NFS, SMB)

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP) — Persistence & File Systems

exercises: Simulate FIFO, Optimal, and LRU page replacement algorithms on a page reference string and compare page-fault counts.
interviewQuestions: What happens step-by-step in hardware and the OS kernel when a program accesses a virtual memory address?
How does a journaling file system like ext4 recover quickly after an unexpected power loss?
topics.interviewRelevance: Core CS fundamentals question; directly connects to LRU cache design and database storage engines.
topics.completionCriteria: Can trace a virtual address lookup (TLB -> Page Table -> Disk Page Fault) and explain journaling file systems.

topics.title: Computer Networks, TCP/IP, DNS & HTTP
topics.summary: Covers the OSI & TCP/IP models, TCP vs. UDP (3-way handshake, flow/congestion control), DNS resolution, sockets, RPC, and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and TLS.
topics.whyImportant: Every web request, API call, and microservice interaction traverses DNS, TCP/UDP, TLS, and HTTP.

subtopics.name: TCP/IP stack & OSI model layers
TCP vs. UDP: 3-way handshake, reliability, flow control, congestion control, and QUIC/UDP use cases
DNS (Domain Name System): hierarchical resolution process, record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, NS), and TTL caching
HTTP protocol: Request methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), Status codes (2xx–5xx), headers, HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3
Client-server architecture, OS Sockets, WebSockets, and Remote Procedure Call (RPC / gRPC)

resources.title: MDN Web Docs — HTTP Reference & Status Codes

exercises: Inspect a live HTTPS request using `curl -v` or browser DevTools to trace DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and HTTP headers.
Build a minimal multi-client TCP echo or chat server using sockets.
interviewQuestions: What happens step-by-step when you type `https://example.com` into a browser and press Enter?
Compare TCP and UDP: why do video streaming, gaming, and HTTP/3 (QUIC) use UDP?
topics.interviewRelevance: The 'What happens when you type a URL' question and TCP vs. UDP / REST vs. gRPC are universal interview classics.
topics.completionCriteria: Can trace the end-to-end lifecycle of an HTTPS request from DNS resolution to socket teardown.

topics.title: Relational Databases (SQL), Normalization & Transactions
topics.summary: Covers relational schema design, constraints, normal forms (1NF–BCNF), SQL DDL/DML/DQL/DCL, Joins, Window Functions, ACID properties, and Transaction Isolation Levels.
topics.whyImportant: Relational databases remain the default transactional store for business-critical software; SQL and ACID isolation are tested in both coding and system design rounds.

subtopics.name: Relational schema constraints (Primary Key, Foreign Key, Unique, Check, Default) & Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF)
SQL Queries (DQL): Joins (Inner, Left/Right/Full Outer, Cross), GROUP BY/HAVING, Subqueries, and Window Functions
SQL DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE/UPSERT, TRUNCATE), and DCL (GRANT, REVOKE)
Transactions & ACID Properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) with COMMIT/ROLLBACK
Transaction Isolation Levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable (dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads)
Views, Materialized Views, Stored Procedures, Functions, and Triggers (BEFORE/AFTER)

exercises: Design a normalized 3NF e-commerce schema (users, products, orders, order_items, payments) and write analytical queries using Joins and `ROW_NUMBER() / RANK()` window functions.
Open two concurrent psql/MySQL sessions to reproduce a dirty read, lost update, or phantom read under different isolation levels.
interviewQuestions: Explain the 4 ACID properties and how write-ahead logging (WAL) and MVCC implement them.
What concurrency anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, write skew) occur at each SQL isolation level?
topics.interviewRelevance: SQL query writing, schema normalization, and transaction isolation levels are staple backend interview topics.
topics.completionCriteria: Can write complex Joins/Window functions, normalize schemas to 3NF/BCNF, and explain SQL isolation levels.

topics.title: Database Indexing & Query Optimization
topics.summary: Covers B-Tree and B+ Tree indexes, clustered vs. non-clustered indexes, composite indexes (leftmost prefix rule), bitmap indexes, covering indexes, and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` query plans.
topics.whyImportant: Bad indexing is the #1 cause of database bottlenecks in production systems; interviewers regularly ask how to optimize slow queries.

subtopics.name: B-Tree vs. B+ Tree storage internals and Clustered vs. Secondary indexes
Composite Indexes, column ordering (leftmost prefix rule), and Covering Indexes
Bitmap Indexing, Hash Indexing, and Full-Text / Inverted Indexes
Query execution plans (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`), index selectivity, and write-amplification trade-offs

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke! — SQL Indexing & Tuning Guide

exercises: Seed a table with 1,000,000 rows, run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a multi-column filter+sort query before and after adding a composite index.
interviewQuestions: If you create a composite index on `(user_id, created_at)`, which queries can use it and why does a query filtering only on `created_at` miss the index?
Why does adding too many indexes slow down `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` operations?
topics.interviewRelevance: Directly tested in backend engineering and system design interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can design composite indexes for query access patterns and read `EXPLAIN` plans to eliminate sequential scans.

topics.title: NoSQL Databases (Key-Value, Document, Column-Family, Graph)
topics.summary: Covers the 4 NoSQL categories—Key-Value (Redis/DynamoDB), Document (MongoDB), Wide-Column (Cassandra), and Graph (Neo4j)—plus LSM-Trees vs. B-Trees and SQL vs. NoSQL selection criteria.
topics.whyImportant: System design interviews require choosing the right storage engine (SQL, Document, Key-Value, Columnar, or Graph) for each workload's read/write/consistency profile.

subtopics.name: Key-Value stores (Redis, DynamoDB): in-memory caching, partition keys, TTLs
Document databases (MongoDB): schema flexibility, embedding vs. referencing, indexing
Column-family stores (Cassandra, Bigtable): LSM-Trees, SSTables, high write throughput, time-series
Graph databases (Neo4j): traversal-heavy social/recommendation relationships
SQL vs. NoSQL decision framework and ACID vs. BASE trade-offs

resources.title: System Design Primer — SQL vs. NoSQL

exercises: Compare schema and query patterns for a chat message history store in PostgreSQL vs. Cassandra/DynamoDB vs. MongoDB.
interviewQuestions: When would you choose a wide-column store (Cassandra) or DynamoDB over PostgreSQL?
Compare B+ Trees (read-optimized) with LSM-Trees + SSTables (write-optimized) used in NoSQL engines.
topics.interviewRelevance: Required in every System Design interview when justifying storage layer choices.
topics.completionCriteria: Can justify when to use Relational, Key-Value, Document, Wide-Column, or Graph databases based on access patterns.

phases.title: Phase 4: Software Development and Engineering
phases.subtitle: Git, Linux CLI, SDLC, Clean Code, SOLID principles, Testing, APIs, and Application Architecture
phases.summary: Brings together Version Control (Section 15), Software Development Methodologies, Coding Best Practices (Section 9), Software Testing Foundations (Section 14), and Application Architecture (Section 12) so learners can build, test, and structure real-world services.
phases.whyThisOrder: Before designing complex object models (Phase 5) or distributed architectures (Phase 6), an engineer needs mastery of Git, CLI workflows, clean code/SOLID, automated testing, and REST/RPC API design.

topics.title: Git & Version Control Workflows
topics.originalSection: 15. Version control System / 9. Problem-solving and Coding
topics.summary: Covers Git internals (commits, trees, blobs, refs), branching strategies, merge vs. rebase, conflict resolution, `git bisect`, and pull request code review workflows.
topics.whyImportant: Version control and collaborative code review are daily engineering essentials.

subtopics.name: Git fundamentals: staging, commits, branches, HEAD, and remote tracking (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)
Git Merge vs. Git Rebase, squash commits, cherry-pick, reflog, and resolving merge conflicts
Collaborative workflows: trunk-based development, feature branches, and code reviews

exercises: Practice interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`), resolve a simulated merge conflict, and recover a dropped commit using `git reflog`.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase`, and why should you never rebase a shared public branch?
How does `git bisect` help locate a regression commit in O(log N) steps?
topics.interviewRelevance: Tested in practical engineering discussions and take-home/pair-programming rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can branch, rebase interactively, resolve conflicts, and use `reflog`/`bisect` confidently.

topics.title: Linux, Shell & Command-Line Fundamentals
topics.summary: Covers POSIX file permissions, standard streams (stdin/stdout/stderr), pipes, process management (`ps`, `top`, `kill`), network diagnostics (`curl`, `netstat`/`ss`, `dig`), and text processing.
topics.whyImportant: Backend servers, containers, and CI runners run on Linux; CLI fluency is crucial for debugging production systems.

subtopics.name: File navigation, permissions (`chmod`, `chown`), symlinks, and standard streams/pipes (`|`, `>`, `2>&1`)
Text & log inspection (`grep`, `awk`, `sed`, `jq`, `tail -f`, `less`)
Process, memory, disk, and network diagnostics (`ps`, `top`, `lsof`, `df`, `du`, `curl`, `ss`)

exercises: Write a shell pipeline that parses an NGINX access log to find the top 10 IP addresses causing HTTP 500 errors.
interviewQuestions: How would you diagnose a Linux server that is running out of disk space even though `du` shows low file usage (hint: deleted open file descriptors via `lsof`)?
How do you find which process is listening on port 8080 and terminate it gracefully?
topics.interviewRelevance: Frequently asked in backend, DevOps/SRE, and production debugging interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can inspect logs, diagnose CPU/memory/port issues, and chain shell commands comfortably.

topics.title: SDLC, Clean Code & SOLID Principles
topics.originalSection: 6. Low-Level Design / 9. Problem-solving and Coding / 13. System Design
topics.summary: Consolidates duplicated coverage of Clean Code, DRY, KISS, YAGNI, Law of Demeter, Cohesion/Coupling, and the 5 SOLID principles from Sections 6, 9, and 13.
topics.whyImportant: Interviewers grade coding and LLD rounds heavily on modularity, naming, separation of concerns, and adherence to SOLID principles.

subtopics.name: Code readability, naming conventions, modularity, high cohesion, and loose coupling
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple), YAGNI, and Law of Demeter
Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) & Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) & Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), Dependency Injection, and Inversion of Control
Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC): Agile, iterative delivery, and code review culture

exercises: Refactor a 200-line 'God class' order processor that violates SRP, OCP, and DIP into clean, testable services.
interviewQuestions: Give a concrete code example of a Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) violation (such as Square inheriting from Rectangle) and how to fix it.
How does Dependency Inversion (DIP) make unit testing with mocks possible?
topics.interviewRelevance: Directly evaluated in every Low-Level Design and machine-coding interview.
topics.completionCriteria: Can spot SOLID violations in existing code and refactor toward clean interfaces and dependency injection.

topics.title: Software Testing Foundations & Quality Engineering
topics.originalSection: 14. Testing, Reliability & Observability / 9. Problem-solving and Coding
topics.summary: Covers the testing pyramid (unit, integration, E2E), test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes, spies), contract testing, database integration testing, and property-based testing.
topics.whyImportant: Writing testable code and verifying edge cases separates senior engineering candidates from pure competitive programmers.

subtopics.name: Unit, integration, end-to-end (E2E), and acceptance tests; Testing Pyramid vs. Testing Trophy
Test doubles: Mocks, stubs, fakes, spies, and deterministic fixtures
Test coverage metrics and their limitations; boundary-value analysis
API contract tests (consumer-driven contracts), database migration tests, and Testcontainers
Concurrency tests, fault injection, idempotency tests, and property-based/fuzz testing

resources.title: Tech Interview Handbook — Software Engineering Best Practices

exercises: Write unit tests with mocked external dependencies and an integration test suite for a REST service.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between a Mock, a Stub, and a Fake, and when can over-mocking make tests brittle?
Why can 95% line coverage still miss critical production bugs?
topics.interviewRelevance: Tested in machine coding, LLD, and backend engineering interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can design unit and integration tests using mocks/fakes and test boundary/failure cases systematically.

topics.title: API Development & Application Architecture
topics.summary: Covers RESTful API design, idempotency, pagination, versioning, gRPC/GraphQL comparison, Layered Architecture (Presentation, Business Logic, Data Access), and monolith vs. SOA.
topics.whyImportant: Clean API design and layered service architecture bridge single-process code and multi-service High-Level Design.

subtopics.name: RESTful API design: resource naming, HTTP verbs, status codes, pagination (cursor vs. offset), filtering
API Versioning (URI, header, query), Idempotency keys, and safe retries
REST vs. gRPC (Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2 streaming) vs. GraphQL trade-offs
Layered Architecture: Presentation, Business Logic, Data Access (Repository), and Cross-cutting concerns
Monolithic Architecture vs. Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) & 12-Factor App principles

resources.title: System Design Primer — API & Application Architecture
ByteByteGo System Design 101 — REST vs. gRPC vs. GraphQL

exercises: Design and build a layered REST API (Controller -> Service -> Repository) with cursor-based pagination, input validation, and idempotency keys.
interviewQuestions: Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over `OFFSET / LIMIT` pagination on large tables?
How do you make a `POST /payments` API endpoint idempotent so network retries never double-charge a user?
topics.interviewRelevance: API contract design and idempotency are asked in virtually every HLD and backend interview.
topics.completionCriteria: Can design REST/gRPC API contracts with pagination, versioning, and idempotency guarantees.

phases.title: Phase 5: Low-Level Design (LLD)
phases.subtitle: Object-oriented domain modeling, UML diagrams, GoF design patterns, and classic LLD interview problems
phases.summary: Unifies all Low-Level Design content from Section 6 and removes the duplicate Design Patterns lists previously scattered in Sections 10 and 13.
phases.whyThisOrder: LLD applies OOP (Phase 1), data structures (Phase 2), concurrency (Phase 3), and SOLID principles (Phase 4) to design extensible, thread-safe software components before scaling to multi-machine HLD (Phase 6).

topics.title: Requirements Clarification, Domain Modeling & UML
topics.summary: Covers translating ambiguous requirements into entities, value objects, aggregates, invariants, and communicating designs with UML Class, Sequence, and State Machine diagrams.
topics.whyImportant: LLD interviews test how systematically you clarify scope, identify core entities, and communicate relationships before writing code.

subtopics.name: Clarify functional/non-functional requirements and define extension points without overengineering
Identify entities, value objects, aggregates, invariants, and object lifecycles
UML Class Diagrams: association, aggregation, composition, inheritance, realization
UML Sequence Diagrams (method calls, async boundaries) & State Machine Diagrams (transitions, guards)

exercises: Draw a UML Class Diagram and State Machine Diagram for a Vending Machine and an Order Fulfillment workflow.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between Aggregation and Composition in a UML Class Diagram?
How do you decide which requirements to model as interfaces vs. concrete classes in a 45-minute LLD interview?
topics.interviewRelevance: First 10–15 minutes of every LLD/OOD interview.
topics.completionCriteria: Can turn a problem prompt into a clean entity model and UML class/state diagram within 10 minutes.

topics.title: Design Patterns in Practice (Creational, Structural, Behavioral)
topics.originalSection: 6. Low-Level Design / 10. Programming Languages / 13. System Design (Deduplicated)
topics.summary: Consolidates all Creational, Structural, and Behavioral design patterns into one authoritative module focused on practical applicability and knowing when NOT to force a pattern.
topics.whyImportant: Patterns like Strategy, Factory, Observer, Builder, State, and Decorator solve recurring extensibility problems in LLD interviews and production codebases.

subtopics.name: Creational Patterns: Factory / Abstract Factory (P0), Builder (P1), Singleton & thread-safety pitfalls (P1), Prototype (P2)
Behavioral Patterns: Strategy (P0), Observer / Pub-Sub (P0), State (P1), Command (P1), Chain of Responsibility, Iterator, Template Method
Structural Patterns: Adapter / Facade (P1), Decorator / Proxy (P1), Composite (P1), Bridge, Flyweight
Anti-overengineering: Recognize when NOT to introduce a design pattern

resources.title: Refactoring.Guru — The Catalog of Design Patterns

exercises: Implement a pluggable Notification Service using Factory + Strategy + Decorator (for retry/logging wrappers).
Implement an Order workflow using the State pattern instead of nested `if/else` status checks.
interviewQuestions: How does the Strategy pattern eliminate `switch/if-else` chains and satisfy the Open/Closed Principle?
Why is the Singleton pattern often considered an anti-pattern for testing, and how does Dependency Injection replace it?
topics.interviewRelevance: Core backbone of LLD interviews; Strategy, Factory, Observer, State, and Decorator appear in almost every problem.
topics.completionCriteria: Can implement top 8 design patterns from memory and justify trade-offs without forcing patterns unnecessarily.

topics.title: Component Design, Persistence Boundaries & Thread Safety
topics.summary: Covers interface-first component contracts, Repository / Unit of Work patterns, fine-grained locking, immutability, atomic operations, and handling mid-interview requirement changes.
topics.whyImportant: Senior LLD rounds always probe concurrency (e.g., two users booking the same movie seat simultaneously) and schema/extensibility trade-offs.

subtopics.name: Interface-first design, stable public contracts, and dependency injection for testability
Repository / Unit of Work patterns, data access layering, and transaction boundaries
Thread safety in LLD: fine-grained locks, read-write locks, concurrent maps, immutability, race prevention
Demonstrating a requirement change without rewriting the core design

resources.title: Refactoring.Guru — Design Patterns in Java & Python

exercises: Write a thread-safe Seat Booking Manager that prevents double-booking under 50 concurrent reservation threads.
interviewQuestions: How do you prevent two threads from booking the same parking spot or theater seat without locking the entire building?
How do you structure your classes so switching from an in-memory store to a SQL database requires zero changes to business logic?
topics.interviewRelevance: Differentiates mid-level and senior candidates in LLD and machine coding rounds.
topics.completionCriteria: Can write thread-safe, interface-driven domain services that cleanly adapt to follow-up requirement changes.

topics.title: Classic Low-Level Design (LLD) Interview Problems
topics.summary: Hands-on practice across all 12 classic LLD problems from the repository: LRU/LFU Cache, Parking Lot, Rate Limiter, Logging Framework, Notification Service, Elevator, Movie Booking, Splitwise, Vending Machine, In-Memory File System, Chess/Tic-Tac-Toe, and Library Management.
topics.whyImportant: Practicing full 45-minute LLD simulations builds the speed needed to define models, apply patterns, and write compilable code under time constraints.

subtopics.name: Design a Cache with LRU / LFU eviction policies (HashMap + Doubly Linked List)
Design a Rate Limiter (Strategy interface for Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Sliding Window)
Design a Parking Lot (spot types, pricing strategies, tickets, concurrent entry gates)
Design a Logging Framework (appenders, log levels, thread safety) & Notification Framework (channels, retries)
Design an In-Memory File System (Composite/Trie directory tree)
Design a Movie Ticket Booking System (seat locking with TTL expiry) & Splitwise Expense Sharing System
Design an Elevator System (dispatch scheduling), Vending Machine (State pattern), Chess/Tic-Tac-Toe, and Library System

exercises: Implement compilable, unit-tested solutions for: (1) LRU Cache, (2) Pluggable Rate Limiter, (3) Parking Lot, and (4) Movie Ticket Seat Locking.
interviewQuestions: Design a Parking Lot that supports motorcycles, cars, and buses, multiple entry gates, and pluggable hourly/flat-rate pricing.
Design an extensible Rate Limiter library supporting per-user and per-IP quotas with swap-in algorithms.
topics.interviewRelevance: Directly mirrors 100% of OOD/LLD and machine coding interview prompts.
topics.completionCriteria: Can complete requirement scoping, class diagramming, and core working code for any of the 12 classic LLD problems in 45 minutes.

phases.title: Phase 6: High-Level Design (HLD) and System Design
phases.subtitle: Scalability, caching, message queues, database scaling, distributed systems, CAP theorem, and HLD case studies
phases.summary: Unifies System Architecture (Section 12), System Design (Section 13), Cloud Messaging (Section 3), Distributed File Systems (Section 8), and the 76-question `System Design/Microservices.md` guide, while adding missing CAP/PACELC and classic HLD case studies.
phases.whyThisOrder: High-Level Design synthesizes networking (Phase 3), databases/NoSQL (Phase 3), APIs (Phase 4), and component design (Phase 5) to architect distributed systems serving millions of requests.

topics.title: Scalability, Load Balancing, CDNs & API Gateways
topics.summary: Covers horizontal vs. vertical scaling, stateless service tiers, Consistent Hashing, L4 vs. L7 Load Balancing, DNS/Anycast routing, CDNs, and API Gateways.
topics.whyImportant: These are the entry-tier building blocks of every system design architecture diagram.

subtopics.name: Horizontal vs. Vertical scaling, Stateless vs. Stateful services, and Auto-scaling
Consistent Hashing: hash ring, virtual nodes, and minimizing key remapping on node churn
Load Balancing: L4 (TCP) vs. L7 (HTTP), Round Robin, Least Connections, Adaptive algorithms, Health checks
DNS Load Balancing, Anycast routing, and Content Delivery Networks (Push vs. Pull CDNs)
API Gateway: routing, TLS termination, rate limiting, authentication, and request aggregation

resources.title: System Design Primer — Scalability, Load Balancers & CDNs
System Design Interview by Alex Xu (Repository Reference)

exercises: Implement a Consistent Hashing ring with virtual nodes in code and measure key movement when adding/removing 1 of 10 nodes.
interviewQuestions: How does Consistent Hashing with virtual nodes solve the rehashing storm problem when a cache node crashes?
What is the difference between a Layer 4 Load Balancer, a Layer 7 Load Balancer, and an API Gateway?
topics.interviewRelevance: Used in the first 15 minutes of every High-Level System Design interview.
topics.completionCriteria: Can diagram edge-to-service traffic flow (DNS -> CDN -> L7 LB -> API Gateway -> Stateless Services) and explain Consistent Hashing.

topics.title: Distributed Caching, Message Queues & Event-Driven Architecture
topics.originalSection: 12. System Architecture / 13. System Design / 3. Cloud Messaging (Deduplicated)
topics.summary: Consolidates duplicated caching and messaging sections into one module covering Cache-Aside, Write-Through/Write-Behind, cache stampede mitigation, RabbitMQ/SQS vs. Kafka/Kinesis, DLQs, and backpressure.
topics.whyImportant: Caching scales read-heavy workloads by 10–100x; asynchronous message queues decouple write-heavy and bursty workloads.

subtopics.name: Caching Strategies: Cache-Aside, Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind (Write-Back), and Refresh-Ahead
Cache Eviction, Invalidation, Hot Keys, and Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd prevention (mutex locks, jittered TTLs)
Message Queues (SQS, RabbitMQ): standard vs. FIFO, visibility timeout, retries, poison messages, Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ)
Event-Driven Architecture & Streaming (Apache Kafka, Kinesis, SNS/EventBridge): pub/sub fan-out, consumer groups, offset retention
Delivery guarantees (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), deduplication, and backpressure

resources.title: System Design Primer — Cache & Asynchronous Queues
Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann (Repository Reference)

exercises: Design a cache layer that prevents cache stampede on hot keys and handles database-cache consistency during writes.
interviewQuestions: Compare Cache-Aside vs. Write-Through vs. Write-Behind caching: what are the consistency and data-loss risks of each?
When do you choose a log-based event stream like Kafka over a traditional message queue like RabbitMQ or SQS?
topics.interviewRelevance: Redis caching strategies and Kafka/SQS queue trade-offs appear in nearly 90% of HLD interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can select the right caching pattern and message broker (SQS vs. Kafka) and handle hot keys, stampedes, and poison messages.

topics.title: Database Scaling: Replication, Partitioning (Sharding) & Distributed Storage
topics.summary: Covers read replicas, leader-follower/multi-leader/leaderless replication, horizontal sharding strategies, hot shards, cross-shard joins, and distributed file/object systems (HDFS, Ceph, S3).
topics.whyImportant: The stateful data tier is the hardest part of any system to scale horizontally.

subtopics.name: Replication: Single-Leader (Leader-Follower), Multi-Leader, and Leaderless (Dynamo-style quorum R + W > N)
Replication lag anomalies and Consistency models (Read-after-write, Monotonic reads, Eventual consistency)
Partitioning / Sharding: Range-based vs. Hash-based sharding, directory-based routing, and hot-partition mitigation
Distributed File & Object Storage: HDFS, Ceph, and S3 object storage architecture (moved from OS section)

resources.title: System Design Primer — Database Replication & Sharding

exercises: Design a sharding key and hot-celebrity mitigation strategy for a 500M-user social media posts table.
interviewQuestions: How do you handle replication lag when a user updates their profile and immediately refreshes the page (read-your-own-writes)?
What causes a 'hot shard' (celebrity problem) in a hash-partitioned database, and how do key salting or read caches fix it?
topics.interviewRelevance: Sharding keys, replication lag, and quorum math are central to senior system design interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can choose partition keys, calculate quorum consistency (R + W > N), and mitigate replication lag and hot partitions.

topics.title: Microservices, Distributed Systems & CAP / Consensus
topics.originalSection: 12. System Architecture / 13. System Design / System Design/Microservices.md
topics.summary: Covers CAP & PACELC theorems, consensus & leader election (Raft/Paxos), distributed transactions (Saga choreography vs. orchestration, 2PC, Outbox pattern), CQRS, Event Sourcing, Circuit Breakers, Service Mesh, and the preserved 76 Microservices Interview Q&A.
topics.whyImportant: Distributed systems trade off consistency, availability, and latency under network partitions; mastering these trade-offs is the core of HLD.

subtopics.name: CAP Theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance) & PACELC Theorem (Latency vs. Consistency)
ACID vs. BASE, Eventual Consistency, and Consensus / Leader Election (Paxos, Raft, ZooKeeper/etcd)
Microservices Patterns: Service Discovery, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Sidecar, Service Mesh (Istio/Linkerd), Strangler Fig
Distributed Transactions: Two-Phase Commit (2PC), Saga Pattern (Choreography vs. Orchestration), Transactional Outbox
Event Sourcing & CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
Top 76 Microservices Architecture Interview Questions (Preserved from `System Design/Microservices.md`)

resources.title: Microservices Architecture & Top 76 Q&A (Original Repository Guide)
System Design Primer — Microservices & CAP Theorem

exercises: Design an Order -> Payment -> Inventory Saga workflow using both Choreography and Orchestration, detailing compensating rollback actions for each failure step.
interviewQuestions: In a distributed system experiencing a network partition, explain why you must choose between CP and AP, and give a real banking vs. social feed example.
How does the Saga pattern with a Transactional Outbox maintain eventual consistency across microservices without 2-Phase Commit locks?
topics.interviewRelevance: Directly tested in all mid-level, senior, and staff HLD interviews.
topics.completionCriteria: Can defend CP vs. AP choices, design Saga workflows, and answer the repository's 76 microservices architecture questions.

topics.title: Practical System Design (HLD) Interview Case Studies
topics.originalSection: 13. System Design (Expanded with Practical Interview Case Studies)
topics.summary: Applies back-of-the-envelope capacity estimation (QPS, bandwidth, storage, p95 latency) and end-to-end architecture design to the most frequently asked HLD interview problems.
topics.whyImportant: System Design interviews require structuring a 45-minute deep dive from requirements and capacity math to APIs, data model, high-level diagram, and bottleneck resolution.
